paragraphs.heading: The Red Planet
paragraphs.text: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, nicknamed the Red Planet for its orange-red color. It is a desert-like rocky world with a thin atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide (CO₂). At average surface level the air pressure is just a few thousandths of Earth's, the air temperature runs from −153 to 20 °C, and cosmic radiation is high. Some water remains, in the ground, as thin clouds, fog and frost, and in permafrost and ice caps. But there are no lakes or seas of liquid water on the surface.

paragraphs.heading: Size, seasons and moons
paragraphs.text: Mars is about half as wide as Earth, at 6,779 km, and its surface area is close to all of Earth's dry land put together. Its surface gravity is about a third of Earth's. With gravity this low, even the weak wind lifts fine dust and spreads it over the ground and through the air. Mars is tilted on its axis by 25 degrees, so it has seasons, like Earth with its 23.5-degree tilt. A Martian year lasts 687 Earth days, a day, called a sol, lasts 24.6 hours, and two small, irregular moons, Phobos and Deimos, circle the planet.

paragraphs.heading: A world of two halves
paragraphs.text: The land divides roughly into north and south, a pattern called the Martian dichotomy: flat, low plains in the north and cratered highlands in the south. One idea is that a Pluto-sized body struck Mars about four billion years ago, and that this impact caused the split. It is thought to have carved the smooth Borealis basin, which covers 40% of the planet. Mars also has huge extinct volcanoes, the tallest being Olympus Mons at 21.9 km, and Valles Marineris, a canyon 4,000 km long. Marsquakes show the planet is fairly active underground.

paragraphs.heading: Three chapters of history
paragraphs.text: Mars formed along with the other planets about 4.5 billion years ago. In the Noachian period, from 4.5 to 3.5 billion years ago, the surface took meteor impacts, valleys formed, erosion went on, oceans may have existed, and the planet lost its magnetosphere. The Hesperian period that followed brought widespread volcanic activity and floods that cut immense outflow channels. The Amazonian period continues today. Because of this history, whether life ever existed on Mars, or exists now, is still being actively studied.

paragraphs.heading: Visiting Mars
paragraphs.text: The first flight to Mars, Mars 1 in 1963, lost contact on the way. Mariner 4 made the first successful flyby in 1965. In 1971 Mariner 9 went into orbit there, the first spacecraft to orbit any body besides the Moon, Sun or Earth, and that same year Mars 3 made the first successful landing. Probes have been working at Mars without a break since 1997. At times more than ten have operated together, more than at any other planet beyond Earth.

paragraphs.heading: A ring that may have been
paragraphs.text: A 2023 study used the tilt of Deimos's orbit to argue that Mars may once have had a ring system, between 3.5 and 4 billion years ago. The ring may have come from an earlier moon with 20 times the mass of Phobos. If so, Phobos itself would be a leftover of the ring.
